title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers are using AI-generated deepfakes and voice clones to impersonate trusted individuals and steal money from victims in Georgia and South Florida. The impersonations target vulnerable populations, including immigrants deceived by fake immigration attorneys and families targeted by elaborated versions of the grandparent scam. This is a failure of trust in communications systems where the person receiving a call or message cannot verify the identity of the sender through their usual methods.

The vulnerability lies in the gap between how people authenticate others in everyday life and how easily audio and visual identity markers can now be replicated. A person hearing a familiar voice or seeing a known person's photograph has historically been sufficient proof of identity, but AI systems can now forge both. Catching this would require institutions and individuals to verify requests through independent channels before acting, since the primary channel of communication is now unreliable.

It is not established what role, if any, social media platforms or communication services played in enabling these scams, or what steps they have taken in response.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and voice clones to steal money from victims across Georgia and South Florida. The FBI reported that Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams in 2025, with criminals impersonating trusted individuals through fake voices, photos, and phone calls. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose identity was cloned to target immigrants and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints totaling $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia experienced 71 complaints resulting in $10.4 million in losses.

Law enforcement officials warn that AI technology makes familiar scams like the grandparent scam harder to detect. Criminals use audio samples from social media to generate convincing emergency calls, claiming relatives need immediate money. Financial institutions are urging customers to verify requests through trusted channels and avoid responding hastily to unexpected communications. Experts recommend establishing family code words for verification and contacting people directly through known phone numbers before sending money, as verification rather than speed provides the strongest defense against these increasingly sophisticated schemes.
